definition: what stops most people improving at the point where I keep going

settled:
Reaching the ceiling of the fast route is what stops the slow one. The skill feels done, and feeling done switches off the deliberate work that would have carried it further.

The plateau is not a limit on how good a person can get. It is the fast route's leftover error switching off the improving.

In me that signal never fires, because the accelerator is reduced. So the deliberate engine keeps running long past where it would ordinarily have stopped.

The difference at the end is a rate of mistakes rather than a height of skill. Put as skill it sounds like nothing. Put as how many slips per hundred are left, it reads correctly.

There is no one fast system to be missing either. Some routes work in me and some do not, so saying my compensations are effortful forever is right about the broken ones and wrong about the rest.

The pattern is not general. It shows up where a thing leans on picking up social rules or on chunking a sequence, rather than across all learning.

title: Why The Slow Route Ends Higher
